reception.text: The gift drew applause and no controversy: it cost the treasury nothing and made a private donor the hero.
John Muir wrote Kent that the gift was "in many ways the most notable service to God & man I've heard of since my forest wanderings began."
reception.source: John Muir to William Kent, February 6, 1908, Kent Family Papers, Yale, MS 309

reception.text: Roosevelt offered to name the monument for Kent; Kent declined, and Roosevelt replied, "By George! you are right."
reception.source: Roosevelt to Kent, January 22 and February 5, 1908; Kent to Roosevelt, January 30, 1908

political_impact.text: The North Coast Water Company pressed its condemnation suit for nearly a year after the land became federal, but Kent was never served and the suit was never tried.
political_impact.source: Elizabeth Thacher Kent, "Biography of William Kent, Independent" (c. 1950); letter of Kent's law firm, December 21, 1908

political_impact.text: Interior Secretary Garfield approved no funding for the monument for more than nine months while the suit hung over it.
Kent asked Roosevelt to have the district attorney "use every possible means to prevent the destruction of a single tree," and Roosevelt answered at once.
The water company engineered a four-day water shortage in Mill Valley to build pressure; residents saw it was deliberate and it backfired.

legacy.text: Muir Woods was the tenth national monument and the first established on land donated to the United States under the Antiquities Act.
legacy.source: Ronald F. Lee, The Story of the Antiquities Act

legacy.text: As a congressman, Kent became a leading champion of the 1913 Raker Act damming Yosemite's Hetch Hetchy Valley, a break that cost him Muir's friendship.
legacy.source: research entry; Kent to Rep. Sydney Anderson, July 2, 1913

legacy.text: Delegates to the United Nations founding conference held a memorial to Franklin Roosevelt in Cathedral Grove; no proclamation or order designated the site.
It is the only old-growth coast redwood forest in the San Francisco Bay Area, with 756,573 recreation visits in 2025.

today.name: Muir Woods National Monument
today.note: The only old-growth coast redwood forest in the San Francisco Bay Area.

uncertain: Why the proclamation calls the Kents "of the City of Chicago" when they had moved to Kentfield, California, in 1907 is not known.
The sent wording of Muir's February 6, 1908 letter rests on NPS transcriptions of the undigitized original at Yale.
